title: Incremental S3 Processing
prompt: Parquet files are added to S3 every day. You run a Glue ETL job on a schedule and want to process new and changed objects compared with the previous successful run of the same job. You do not want to manage custom checkpoints, and new and changed files can be identified by their modification times.

choices.text: Only rerun the Glue crawler before the job
choices.explanation: This can update the schema, but it does not maintain the processing state for each job run.

choices.text: Change the Glue Data Catalog database name
choices.explanation: Changing the metadata name does not track which inputs have already been processed.

choices.text: Enable Glue job bookmarks
choices.explanation: They record input-processing state and support incremental processing for supported sources.

choices.text: Control ETL inputs with S3 Versioning
choices.explanation: Version retention and the job's processing position are separate functions.

learning.reason: They record input-processing state and support incremental processing for supported sources.
learning.concept: Job bookmarks track the input side; deduplication of write results requires separate design.

category: データ取り込み・変換・運用
title: Athena Data Scanned
prompt: Audit logs arrive in S3 every day. Typical Athena queries always specify a date range and read only a few columns from a wide schema. You want to reduce the amount scanned by both date and column while continuing to use existing SQL.

choices.text: Use Parquet with date partitioning
choices.explanation: This enables partition pruning and column selection.

choices.text: Compress a single CSV file with gzip
choices.explanation: Compression is possible, but this does not provide date partitioning or column-level reads.

choices.text: Use a date-partitioned text format
choices.explanation: The date can be filtered, but a columnar format is appropriate for reading only the required columns.

choices.text: Enable versioning on the S3 bucket
choices.explanation: Versioning manages object history but does not narrow the query scan range.

learning.reason: This enables partition pruning and column selection.
learning.concept: Filter the partition key in the WHERE clause and specify only the required columns in SELECT.

category: データ取り込み・変換・運用
title: Capturing Updates
prompt: You use Athena engine version 3. From a daily file containing values before and after an update, you need to update the value for an existing key in an Iceberg table and insert rows for new keys. Each key is unique in the input, and you want to apply the changes with a single SQL statement.

choices.text: Use INSERT INTO to add all rows
choices.explanation: Existing rows are not updated, so multiple rows for the same key may remain.

choices.text: Start only a Glue crawler
choices.explanation: A crawler discovers catalog metadata; it does not modify existing rows.

choices.text: Use MERGE INTO with Athena engine version 3
choices.explanation: For a supported Iceberg table, it can express matching, updates, and inserts.

choices.text: Only create a staging table with CTAS
choices.explanation: This does not apply updates or inserts for matching keys in the original table.

learning.reason: For a supported Iceberg table, it can express matching, updates, and inserts.
learning.concept: Verify the update and insert conditions and confirm that keys are not duplicated on the source side before running MERGE.

category: データ取り込み・変換・運用
title: Bulk Loading from S3 to Redshift
prompt: Every night, you output many files of uniform size to S3. You need to load them into Redshift in parallel and persist the data in the warehouse. You will not issue individual INSERT statements from a client.

choices.text: Only run a SELECT in Athena
choices.explanation: This reads query results but does not load data into Redshift.

choices.text: Create only an external table with Redshift Spectrum
choices.explanation: This lets you query data in S3 but does not persist it in an internal warehouse table.

choices.text: Issue an individual INSERT for each row from a client
choices.explanation: This makes it difficult to take advantage of parallel and efficient loading.

choices.text: Use Redshift COPY with S3 as the source
choices.explanation: This uses Redshift's parallel loading capability.

learning.reason: This uses Redshift's parallel loading capability.
learning.concept: Grant the COPY IAM role read access to the input data, and verify the file format and error logging.

category: データ取り込み・変換・運用
title: Table-Level Permissions
prompt: You need to expose only some catalog tables and columns from the same S3 data lake to analysts using Athena. You will not grant users direct access to the original S3 data. You want to manage column definitions centrally rather than copying them.

choices.text: Set an IAM role condition with s3:GetObject for each column
choices.explanation: S3 permissions cannot distinguish fields within a single object.

choices.text: Use Lake Formation data permissions
choices.explanation: In conjunction with supported engines, these permissions can manage access at the table and column levels.

choices.text: Enable KMS key rotation
choices.explanation: Key generation management and column-level access management are separate concerns.

choices.text: Use only an S3 bucket policy
choices.explanation: This handles file access but does not make catalog-level, column-based decisions.

learning.reason: In conjunction with supported engines, these permissions can manage access at the table and column levels.
learning.concept: In addition to logical data-lake permissions, verify that users do not unintentionally retain direct S3 access.

category: データ取り込み・変換・運用
title: A Replayable Stream
prompt: A new Kinesis consumer will be deployed next month, and it must reread seven days of data on Kinesis starting from the deployment point. There is no need to copy all records to separate storage for the new feature. What should be configured now?

choices.text: Enable Enhanced Fan-Out only
choices.explanation: This affects the consumer's read throughput but does not change the retention period.

choices.text: Increase only the number of shards
choices.explanation: This affects processing capacity but does not retain expired records.

choices.text: Only change the consumer's starting position to TRIM_HORIZON
choices.explanation: This can read from the oldest retained record, but it cannot recover data that has exceeded the retention period.

choices.text: Set the stream's retention period to at least seven days
choices.explanation: A new consumer can reread records from sequence positions that remain within the retention period.

learning.reason: A new consumer can reread records from sequence positions that remain within the retention period.
learning.concept: The retention period determines the range that can be reread, while the consumer's processing position is managed separately.

category: データ取り込み・変換・運用
title: Out-of-Order Updates for the Same Key
prompt: Source change events are ingested into Apache Iceberg. Primary keys can be duplicated, events can arrive out of order, and each row has a monotonically increasing sequence from the source. How can you prevent an old redelivery from rolling back a newer value?

choices.text: Deduplicate using only the key and accept the first change to arrive
choices.explanation: This would discard valid changes that arrive later.

choices.text: In staging, retain the maximum sequence for each key and update with MERGE only when it is newer than the existing sequence
choices.explanation: This handles both conflicts within the same batch and old redeliveries across batches.

choices.text: INSERT everything each time and make no changes to reader queries
choices.explanation: Readers would not be able to distinguish the old and new values for the same key.

choices.text: Unconditionally apply the record with the latest reception time
choices.explanation: The latest arrival is not necessarily the latest change in the source.

learning.reason: This handles both conflicts within the same batch and old redeliveries across batches.
learning.concept: Separate processing time from business update order, and retain the version applied to each target row.

category: データ取り込み・変換・運用
title: Stream Aggregation with Late Arrivals
prompt: Clicks are aggregated in five-minute windows. Each event has an occurrence time, and most events arrive within two minutes. A small number of extremely late events will be inspected separately, and state must be restored after a failure or restart.

choices.text: Only extend the stream's retention period
choices.explanation: This increases rereadability, but window timing and state-recovery settings are separate concerns.

choices.text: Keep the windows open indefinitely without using watermarks
choices.explanation: There would be no control over when results become final, and state would continue to grow.

choices.text: Create windows by arrival time and add all records in reception-time order
choices.explanation: Late events would be placed in windows different from their intended event-time windows.

choices.text: Configure Flink event time and watermarks, and set up a separate output for late events and checkpoints
choices.explanation: This closes windows based on occurrence time, allows events beyond the threshold to be inspected, and enables state recovery.

learning.reason: This closes windows based on occurrence time, allows events beyond the threshold to be inspected, and enables state recovery.
learning.concept: Event time, allowed lateness, and state checkpoints are separate controls.

title: Reducing Redistribution for Large Joins
prompt: In Redshift, sales detail data with tens of billions of rows is frequently joined with customer event data with hundreds of millions of rows by customer ID. Customer IDs are evenly distributed, and there is not enough capacity to replicate either table to every node.

choices.text: Use customer ID only as the sort key for both tables
choices.explanation: Changing sort order does not make the data placement match across nodes.

choices.text: Use customer ID as the distribution key for both tables
choices.explanation: Rows with the same join key are placed on the same slice, reducing redistribution during the join.

choices.text: Use ALL distribution for the larger table
choices.explanation: This conflicts with the requirement to avoid replication to every node.

choices.text: Use EVEN distribution for both tables
choices.explanation: This provides even placement but does not guarantee that rows with the same key are colocated.

learning.reason: Rows with the same join key are placed on the same slice, reducing redistribution during the join.
learning.concept: Distribution keys affect redistribution across nodes, while sort keys affect data skipping and processing order.

title: Quarantining Quality Errors
prompt: Rows with missing customer IDs are mixed into the daily ingestion. Normal rows must be published as scheduled, while defective rows must retain the original data and batch ID for root-cause investigation.

choices.text: Record only the row count after publication.
choices.explanation: This does not prevent defective rows from reaching downstream systems and does not identify the problematic rows.

choices.text: Validate required fields before publication, then route passing rows and quarantined output separately.
choices.explanation: This prevents defective data from being mixed in while enabling normal data delivery and subsequent investigation.

choices.text: Discard the entire batch.
choices.explanation: This prevents normal rows from being published and does not preserve data for investigation.

choices.text: Fill in missing IDs with a fixed value and publish every row.
choices.explanation: Unrelated rows could be grouped under the same customer.

learning.reason: This prevents defective data from being mixed in while enabling normal data delivery and subsequent investigation.
learning.concept: For quarantine, retain the original identifiers, the rules applied, and ingestion batch information so the data can be reprocessed.
